items.feedback: Right. The loop is what makes it an agent: the model picks an action, the program runs it, and the result comes back for the next step. A longer prompt or a bigger model only changes what one call can do.

Not quite. You picked (a), but the model doesn't open the booking system; what it actually outputs is check_calendar(machine="laser cutter", date="2026-11-22"), which is option (c). The program is the one that runs it and hands the entries back.

Right. Forty identical failures means more steps add nothing, so you need a stopping condition. A step limit of, say, 40 ends the loop and tells a person what happened, instead of burning time on the same failing edit.

Not quite. Count it like this: question in, call 1 asks for check_calendar; result in, call 2 asks for search_manuals; result in, call 3 asks for check_training_record; result in, call 4 writes the answer. So it's 4, not 1, because the program runs the tools, not the model, as you wrote.

Partly right. "It sends it back to the model" is the what, but you left out the why: the model needs the result in its next input to pick its next step or write the answer. Like when check_calendar returns "laser cutter free at 3 pm" and the model then moves on to the training check.

Partly right. The list of tools with names and descriptions is exactly how it picks, but it doesn't "remember on its own" what it picked before. Say it picks check_calendar on Monday; on Friday it starts fresh with only the tool list the program sends, so the program has to save a student's training status and send it in each time.

summary: You've got the agent loop and how the model picks a tool from descriptions. The thing to fix is who does what: the model only writes requests, and the program runs the tools and feeds results back, and it doesn't remember across sessions on its own. Next, re-trace the laser cutter example from q4 on paper, labelling each step as 'model call' or 'program runs tool'.
